# Zapier Advanced: Multi-Step Zaps, Filters, Paths, and Formatter

## Overview
Real-world automations rarely stop at one action, so this is where Zapier becomes genuinely powerful. Multi-step Zaps let you chain many actions after a single trigger - capture a lead, add it to a CRM, post to Slack, and send a welcome email all from one form submission. To make Zaps smart rather than blindly running every time, you use Filters: a filter checks a condition and only lets the Zap continue if it is met, so you can say 'only continue if the order total is greater than $100' or 'only if the email contains invoice'. When you need different outcomes for different data, you use Paths - Zapier's if/then branching - where Path A runs one set of actions and Path B another, for example routing enterprise leads to sales and small leads to an automated email. The Formatter is your data-transformation toolbox: it can change text case, split and combine strings, do math, reformat dates and times, look up values, and clean messy inputs before they reach the next app - crucial because data from one app rarely arrives in exactly the shape the next app wants. Delays let a Zap wait (send a follow-up email two days later), and scheduling controls timing. Together, multi-step logic, filters, paths, and Formatter turn simple connections into robust automations that handle the real, messy variety of business data - which is exactly what employers expect an automation engineer to build.

## Deep Dive
This module covers: Multi-step Zaps and chaining actions; Filters (only continue if...); Paths (if/then branching); Formatter: text, numbers, dates, and utilities; Delays and scheduling. Mastering these ideas is essential because they appear repeatedly in production AI systems.

### What You Will Learn
- The core theory behind today's topic.
- How to apply it using Python, NumPy, Pandas, or the relevant framework.
- How to evaluate results and avoid common mistakes.
- Where to find authoritative references when you need deeper detail.

### Real-World Context
In industry, these skills are used daily: data scientists clean messy survey data, AI engineers deploy models to REST APIs, and automation engineers orchestrate pipelines. Today's practical task simulates one of these real-world scenarios.

## Hands-On Practice
Practical Task: Extend your Day 6 Zap into a multi-step Zap that adds a filter (only continue for certain submissions) and uses Formatter to reformat a date or capitalize a name before it is saved.
Mini Project: Build a lead-routing Zap using Paths: enterprise leads (company size over a threshold) get added to a CRM and pinged to a sales Slack channel, while small leads receive an automated welcome email - all from one form trigger.
Assignment: Explain the difference between a Filter and a Path, and give a real scenario where you would need each, including what happens to the data in both cases.

Complete all three sections. Each completed section earns points toward your CalibiAI Score. If you are unsure about any part, use the AI assessment popup to submit your work and receive dynamic feedback from DeepSeek.

## Common Mistakes to Avoid
Many beginners rush into coding before fully understanding the data. Others skip validation steps and overestimate model performance. This module helps you build the discipline of checking assumptions first, then applying algorithms systematically.

## Career Impact
The skills covered today are frequently tested in technical interviews and required in entry-level AI engineering roles. Building a portfolio that demonstrates mastery of these concepts will significantly improve your job prospects.

## Key Takeaways
1. Theory guides practice — understand before coding.
2. Clean data and clear metrics are more valuable than complex models.
3. Document your steps for reproducibility.
4. Communication matters: explain results to non-technical stakeholders.

- Read any research papers linked for deeper theory.
- Prepare questions for tomorrow's module.

- Check the GitHub repositories for working code examples.
